title: Graphs and Data Questions: Scales, Best Fit, Trends and Extrapolation | HSC Exam Skills
originalTitle: Graphs and Data Questions: Scales, Best Fit, Trends and Extrapolation | HSC Exam Skills
description:
Lessons and practice: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/
Biology: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/

Graph questions lose marks on the mechanics: uneven scales, missing units, dot-to-dot lines, and trends described without numbers. Learn to read the axes first, draw a graph that earns its marks (TAILS, then a line or curve of best fit), describe a trend with direction, data and any change, read a value between points, and judge a prediction made beyond the data. See a worked Biology question on antibiotic resistance data, then try two training questions, one in Chemistry (fix a student's graph) and one in Biology (describe a relationship). All questions are written for HSCScience in the HSC style; they are not official NESA questions.

Based on patterns in NESA's published HSC marking feedback and marking guidelines for Chemistry and Biology.
Working Scientifically skills content (NSW Biology and Chemistry Stage 6 syllabuses, 2017):
"select qualitative and quantitative data and information and represent them using a range of formats, digital technologies and appropriate media"
"apply quantitative processes where appropriate"
"derive trends, patterns and relationships in data and information"
"assess error, uncertainty and limitations in data"

Previous: Calculation answers that get full marks. Next: Practical questions: fixes that fix. In the Biology playlist, next: Outbreak data and control practice.

The longest HSC science questions can decide your band. Learn how long answers are usually marked, take a question apart into every demand, plan your answer in about a minute with the verdict first, build each paragraph as point, evidence, explain, link, use the stimulus by quoting values and saying what they mean, and finish with a judgement and its condition. Worked example: measles vaccination data and a catch-up program (Biology); drills in Biology and Chemistry. Verdict first, PEEL each paragraph, verdict last. Every question is written for HSCScience in the HSC style; none is an official NESA question.

Based on the NESA glossary of key words (https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/hsc/student-guide/glossary) and patterns in NESA's published HSC marking feedback and marking guidelines for Chemistry and Biology, 2020 to 2025.
Working Scientifically skill: Communicating (NSW Chemistry and Biology Stage 6 syllabuses, 2017): "construct evidence-based arguments and engage in peer feedback to evaluate an argument or conclusion"; Analysing Data and Information: "derive trends, patterns and relationships in data and information".

Previous: Practical questions: validity, reliability, accuracy and fixes that fix. Next in Biology: Evaluate an infectious disease strategy.

title: Mohr Titration: Measuring Chloride with Silver Nitrate and a Chromate Endpoint | Year 12 Chemistry
originalTitle: Mohr Titration: Measuring Chloride with Silver Nitrate and a Chromate Endpoint | Year 12 Chemistry
description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module8/lesson01.sa.html

Chloride can't be seen, and it isn't an acid or a base, so how does a titration find it? See how silver nitrate turns chloride into white silver chloride, why a little potassium chromate gives a red-brown endpoint only once the chloride is nearly gone, and why that order comes from the silver each solid needs, not from which salt is less soluble. Learn the pH window and what acid does to the titre, then turn concordant titres into a chloride concentration in mol/L and g/L. Two exam-style questions at the end.

Chemistry 2017: Year 12 Module 8, Applying Chemical Ideas.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 8):
"conduct investigations and/or process data involving:
- gravimetric analysis
- precipitation titrations"
This video covers precipitation titrations; gravimetric analysis is the next video.
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/chemistry-stage-6-2017

Prerequisites: How does direct titration reveal an unknown concentration? Will mixing these solutions form a precipitate? Next: Gravimetric analysis.

title: Gravimetric Analysis: From Precipitate Mass to Ion Concentration | Year 12 Chemistry
originalTitle: Gravimetric Analysis: From Precipitate Mass to Ion Concentration | Year 12 Chemistry
description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module8/lesson02.sa.html

A clear wastewater sample turns cloudy white when barium ions are added, and the mass of that dried solid tells you how much sulfate was there. See why barium sulfate is chosen over calcium sulfate using Ksp, why the precipitate is digested, washed and dried to constant mass, and how to turn a mass found by difference into a percentage and a concentration. Then learn which errors make the answer too high or too low, and why repeating an analysis doesn't fix them. Two exam-style questions at the end.

Chemistry 2017: Year 12 Module 8, Applying Chemical Ideas.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 8):
"conduct investigations and/or process data involving:
- gravimetric analysis
- precipitation titrations"
This video covers gravimetric analysis; precipitation titrations are in the previous video.
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/chemistry-stage-6-2017

Prerequisites: Ksp expressions and molar solubility; Mohr titration (chloride with silver nitrate). Next: Carry out a gravimetric analysis.

title: Testing for Cations: Flame Tests, Precipitates and Complex Ions | Year 12 Chemistry
originalTitle: Testing for Cations: Flame Tests, Precipitates and Complex Ions | Year 12 Chemistry
description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module8/lesson03.sa.html

Eight bottles have lost their labels. Which metal ion is in each one? Learn a short test sequence that rules ions out one step at a time: dilute hydrochloric acid for silver and lead, dilute sulfuric acid for barium and calcium, then sodium hydroxide for copper, iron(II), iron(III) and magnesium. See why the order matters, why a flame colour supports but doesn't prove, why green iron(II) hydroxide turns brown, and how complex ions with ammonia and thiocyanate confirm the result. Ends on a cation flowchart and two exam-style questions.

Chemistry 2017: Year 12 Module 8, Applying Chemical Ideas.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 8):
"conduct qualitative investigations – using flame tests, precipitation and complexation reactions as appropriate – to test for the presence in aqueous solution of the following ions:
- cations: barium (Ba2+), calcium (Ca2+), magnesium (Mg2+), lead(II) (Pb2+), silver ion (Ag+), copper(II) (Cu2+), iron(II) (Fe2+), iron(III) (Fe3+)
- anions: chloride (Cl–), bromide (Br–), iodide (I–), hydroxide (OH–), acetate (CH3COO–), carbonate (CO32–), sulfate (SO42–), phosphate (PO43–)"
This video covers the cations; the anions are the next video.
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/chemistry-stage-6-2017

Prerequisites: Solubility rules and net ionic equations. Ksp and predicting precipitates. Next: Testing for anions.

title: Testing for Anions: Halides, Sulfate, Carbonate, Phosphate and More | Year 12 Chemistry

description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module8/lesson03.sa.html

The metal ion is copper, but copper what? Learn how to find the anion: dilute acid for carbonate and acetate, acidified barium for sulfate, acidified silver nitrate for chloride, bromide and iodide, with ammonia to tell them apart, neutral silver nitrate for phosphate, and an ammonium test for hydroxide. See why you acidify first, why the wrong acid gives a false positive, and why the order of tests matters. Ends on an anion flowchart and two exam-style questions.

Chemistry 2017: Year 12 Module 8, Applying Chemical Ideas.

- cations: barium (Ba2+), calcium (Ca2+), magnesium (Mg2+), lead(II) (Pb2+), silver ion (Ag+), copper(II) (Cu2+), iron(II) (Fe2+), iron(III) (Fe3+)
- anions: chloride (Cl–), bromide (Br–), iodide (I–), hydroxide (OH–), acetate (CH3COO–), carbonate (CO32–), sulfate (SO42–), phosphate (PO43–)"
This video covers the anions; the cations are the previous video.

title: How Does Negative Feedback Keep Conditions in Range? Homeostasis | Year 12 Biology Module 8
originalTitle: How Does Negative Feedback Keep Conditions in Range? Homeostasis | Year 12 Biology Module 8
description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module8/lesson01.sa.html

You lose heat to the room around you every second, yet your core temperature stays close to 37 °C. Learn what homeostasis means, why body conditions are held within a tolerance range around a set point, and how the five parts of a feedback loop (stimulus, receptor, control centre, effector and response) correct a change. See why the loop is called negative feedback, why the extra response eases as conditions recover, and how positive feedback differs. Then practise constructing a loop from a description and interpreting a temperature graph.

Biology 2017: Year 12 Module 8, Non-infectious Disease and Disorders. Inquiry question: "How is an organism's internal environment maintained in response to a changing external environment?"
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Biology Stage 6, 2017, Module 8):
"construct and interpret negative feedback loops that show homeostasis by using a range of sources, including but not limited to: (ACSBL101, ACSBL110, ACSBL111)" (this video: "temperature (ACSBL098)" and "glucose")
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/biology-stage-6-2017

Next: How do endotherms regulate body temperature?

title: How Do Endotherms Regulate Body Temperature? Feedback and Adaptations | Year 12 Biology Module 8
originalTitle: How Do Endotherms Regulate Body Temperature? Feedback and Adaptations | Year 12 Biology Module 8
description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module8/lesson02.sa.html

In November 2018, a heatwave in far north Queensland killed about 23,000 spectacled flying foxes in two days. Learn how endotherms detect a rise in body temperature, how the hypothalamus uses fast nerve signals and slower hormones such as thyroxine, and how vasodilation and sweating move heat out of the body. Sort temperature adaptations into physiological, behavioural and structural types with the red kangaroo, see trends such as countercurrent heat exchange, and find out why negative feedback has limits. Then practise two HSC-style questions.

Biology 2017: Year 12 Module 8, Non-infectious Disease and Disorders. Inquiry question: "How is an organism's internal environment maintained in response to a changing external environment?"
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Biology Stage 6, 2017, Module 8):
"investigate the various mechanisms used by organisms to maintain their internal environment within tolerance limits, including:" (this video: "trends and patterns in behavioural, structural and physiological adaptations in endotherms that assist in maintaining homeostasis (ACSBL099, ACSBL114)" and "internal coordination systems that allow homeostasis to be maintained, including hormones and neural pathways (ACSBL112, ACSBL113, ACSBL114)")
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/biology-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: How does negative feedback keep conditions in range? Next: Investigating temperature regulation.
